title: Gilgamesh and the Enuma Elish in Their Cuneiform Editions — Haupt's Nimrodepos (1884–91), Jensen's Mythen und Epen (1900), King's Seven Tablets of Creation (1902)

license.payload: Public domain: the tablets are of the first millennium BCE (the Nineveh library, seventh century BCE). Haupt's cuneiform autographs (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1884; 1891), Jensen's Keilinschriftliche Bibliothek VI/1 (Berlin: Reuther, 1900) and King's Seven Tablets of Creation (London: Luzac, 1902) are public domain in the United States (published before 1931). Internet Archive scans of public-domain volumes.

scope: The two great Babylonian poems in the editions that first set them out: Gilgamesh in Haupt's cuneiform and Jensen's transliteration, the Enuma Elish in King's transliteration and copies. George's Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (2003), Lambert's Babylonian Creation Myths (2013) and the electronic Babylonian Library are in copyright or under their own terms and are not seated.
why_seated: The flood story the Bible's flood story answers, a king who seeks to escape death and returns with the knowledge that he cannot, and a creation by the splitting of a body: the oldest written epics of the Near East, beside the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint and the apocalypses on the shelf.
normalization: Internet Archive OCR text layers as fetched, uncorrected (text/<slug>.ocr.txt); the scan under original/<identifier>/ is the witness. Where the text layer is noise over a script (cuneiform, Avestan), the scan is the only reading.
